title: Quantitative evaluation of hindlimb grip strength in mice as a measure of neuromuscular function
author: Zheng, Lunn, et al.

steps.title: Wear PPE and prepare workspace
steps.instruction: Put on gloves and all required personal protective equipment before any handling to avoid contaminating the equipment or animals.

steps.title: Place force gauge in SPF room
steps.instruction: Set the digital force gauge on a level surface inside a small‑animal procedure room that meets Specific Pathogen‑Free (SPF) standards, ensuring controlled air filtration, humidity, and temperature.

steps.title: Adjust gauge height
steps.instruction: Adjust the height of the gauge to a comfortable level for the operator while keeping the sterile environment intact.

steps.title: Attach trapeze bar
steps.instruction: Connect the triangular “trapeze” bar to the digital force gauge as shown in Fig. 1B.

steps.title: Select T‑Peak mode and zero gauge
steps.instruction: Choose the “T‑Peak” mode on the gauge (Fig. 1C) and press the zeroing button (Fig. 1D) so the reading is set to zero before testing any mouse.

steps.title: Prepare data sheet
steps.instruction: Set up a recording sheet (paper or electronic) to log each mouse’s grip‑strength reading and body weight.

steps.title: Measure hindlimb grip strength
steps.instruction: For each mouse, allow it to grasp the trapeze bar with its hindlimbs, gently pull the mouse back until it releases, and record the maximum force that appears immediately after release.

substeps.instruction: Place the mouse in the testing container and let it grasp the bar with both hindlimbs.
Apply a steady, gentle pull on the mouse’s tail until the mouse lets go of the bar.
Watch the gauge display and note the peak force that occurs right after release.
Write the peak force value on the recording sheet.

steps.title: Record mouse body weight
steps.instruction: Weigh the mouse and record its body weight (in grams) on the same sheet after each grip‑strength measurement.

steps.title: Calculate normalized grip strength
steps.instruction: Compute grip strength using the formula: Grip strength (N / g) = Mean digital reading (N) ÷ Body weight (g).

description: Set up digital force gauges.1.Use gloves and other necessary personal protective equipment (PPE) for all following steps to avoid introducing contaminants.2.Place the digital force gauge on a level surface within a designated small animal procedure room that meets Specific Pathogen-Free (SPF) standard (Fig. 1A). Ensure that the room meets all SPF standards, including controlled air filtration, humidity, and temperature, to maintain sterility and reduce contamination risks.Fig. 1Set up of the digital force gauge. (A) Overview of the digital force gauge setup, including the Chatillon DFS3 force gauge and mouse container, placed on a level surface. (B) A triangular “trapeze” bar attachment is connected to the digital force gauge. (C) Location of the “T-Peak” mode on the force gauge. (D) Location of the zeroing feature button on the force gauge.Fig. 13.Adjust the gauge's height according to the operator's preference, keeping the sterile environment during setup.4.Attach the triangular “trapeze” bar to the gauge (Fig. 1B).5.Choose the “T-Peak” mode on the gauge (Fig. 1C) and set the reading to zero before testing the limbs (Fig. 1D).6.Prepare the recording sheet. Using methods described in this study, three trained operators measured the combined grip strength of two-hindlimbs in wild-type adult mice (n = 3). As shown in Fig. 4A, there is no significant difference in combined two-hindlimbs grip strength among operators (p > 0.05). Next, we measured single-hindlimb grip strength. The difference in single-hindlimb grip strength of the same mouse was evident among operators, especially for the left hindlimb. Furthermore, we found that the sum of two single-hindlimb grip strengths is slightly higher than the combined hindlimb grip strength (p > 0.05).Fig. 4Representative measurements of combined and single-hindlimb grip strength.
